Just moved to ATL, completely new to the game, found out it's pretty popular up here, and have a few questions about designing a first character...

First off, I'd suggest getting help to make sure your character is solid. 1st characters can be fun but at the same point they can also ruin your experience.

Tips I wish I would have known:

  • Know which books are allowed

If there are multiple books available, make sure you know which you can use and which you can't to create your character.

  • Pick a theme, not a character.

My first character was a Cleric. Yeah a Cleric. Don't pick this as your first character. It's the equivalent of wanting to play basketball and deciding to join a competitive league. So much more to learn quickly on the fly, that most people have trouble playing them effectively without a TON of help.

I wish someone would have told me to pick a theme instead of a class. A paladin who believes himself to be a fallen deity. A warrior who won't let someone touch him lovingly. An Archer who will always climb a tree to fight. A swashbuckler who likes to dance A LOT.

It completely helps to create a character you enjoy. In a different game (Dungeons the Dragoning) I made my favorite character of all time who was a werewolf who didn't know he was one and who was in search of his family's murderer(it was him.) The amazing thing about it was he was scared to death because he felt he was being hunted because no matter what far galaxy he went, the monster kept on following him.

Because I liked that character's idea, I made the person specifically a certain way. I gave him a lot of strength and agility but not much intellect and wisdom. He therefore was incredibly good in a fight, but would not remember or comprehend that he was the cause of all of his problems. Later on he was going to find out, but unfortunately he died before I could get to that point.

The point is that by creating an idea first, it helps to flesh out your character. So the first thing I would do is create an IDEA.

  • Use online help

People all the time will just say "Character creation is easy, just do this/this/this." But most of the people saying that have been playing for a while. I still spend days thinking about how to make my character do exactly what I want. And then when we get into battles, it ends up never playing out the way I thought it would. This is standard fare I've found.

If you want to play a Warlock, I suggest looking at the forums about Warlocks. Use a site like Myth-Weavers.com or similar to create an character. If you aren't sure about some things, look for a character sheet autofill type file that you can download in order to fill it out.

  • Have fun and be willing to die

It's your first character so you're going to dwell a lot over it. But it's like a rite of passage when you lose your character. Getting rid of that feeling that makes you so enthralled with your character that you are unwilling to play anything else will hold you back. I've had a guy so into his character, who's parents had been killed by dark elves, that he was approached by a high-level wizard disguised as a wood elf and he tried to kill him. I even broke my rule I was so aghast and asked him if he was sure... but when I destroyed him, he quit immediately. Didn't even give me time to explain that he wasn't dead for good, but was in another place.

You will die in this game. It happens. Either your character will die or you and your party will dissolve into party politics and bickering. So instead, be prepared to face death. If it happens, there is often ways to get around it. So be willing to go in with your party and have fun.

If you want to create a specific character with the limited skill options, I like to do it in this order:

Choose your main stat first.

Strength lets you bulldoze things.

Dexterity is good for ranged attacks and "cheating" your way through situations compared to Strength.

Constitution is to make you tankier, and is best used for melee fighters (mages can use it too to hold concentration).

Wisdom gives you "shallow thought". The ability to understand what your instincts are telling you, and how "in tune" you are with your body.

Intelligence gives you "deep thought". The ability to understand the complicated things and to make predictions.

Charisma is your ability to lead or mislead others.

Now, pick a class that matches what you want for your main stat.

Barbarians will almost always want to focus on Strength and Constitution, but can also use Wisdom (to improve their nature-based skills) or Charisma (to improve their frightening presence as a Berserker).

Bards use Charisma as their spellcasting stat, and usually use Dexterity to improve their non-magical abilities, but because of being one of the two "skill monkey" classes they can justify having high enough stats into anything to further improve their skills to better support the group.

Clerics are an interesting sort. Each type of Cleric is vastly different than the last, so how you build them is up to you. First and foremost, Wisdom is your spellcasting modifier. Some Clerics want Constitution to better serve as a defender (like Tempest Clerics). Some want Strength to better bash an enemy's skull in (like a War Cleric). Some might want Charisma to better lead or manipulate people (like Trickster Clerics). Experiment with what you think is right and find out!

Druids use Wisdom as their main stat. If you're a spellcasting type of Druid, Constitution might play a major part. As a transforming Druid, you're borrowing the Constitution of the animal you transform into, so it doesn't play that big of a part. Your intellectual stats (Intelligence, Charisma, Wisdom) carry over as an animal, so consider increasing those as a transforming Druid, or have high physical stats to match the primal ferocity of a beast.

Fighters use primarily Strength and Constitution, but they can also use Dexterity (if they prefer a more agile/ranged type of combat) and Intelligence (in the case of Eldritch Knights, who use magic).

Monks use Dexterity as their main stat for damage and defense, but also use Wisdom to improve their defense and spellcasting power. They tend to be a bit squishy, so don't forget about your Constitution.

Paladins use Strength for damage, Constitution for health, and Charisma for spellcasting. If you plan on being an Avenger Paladin (focuses mostly on vengeance and assassination-style combat), Charisma doesn't play as large of a part as opposed to the Devotion Paladin (guardian/support) or Ancient Paladin (Mobile tanky spellcaster).

Rangers use Dexterity for damage, Constitution for health (more important if going melee), and Wisdom for spellcasting. They have many nature/wisdom based skills, so Wisdom also assists with that, or focus on Dexterity for added tankiness and stealth.

The Rogue uses Dexterity more than anything else. Constitution, as with everyone, increases health. They can also make use of Intelligence for several skills. If you are an Arcane Trickster, Intelligence improves your spellcasting. If you are using the Swashbuckler variant from Unearthed Arcana: Waterborne, you use Charisma to improve your combat abilities.

Both Sorcerors and Warlocks use similar stats, focusing on Charisma. Warlocks might use Dexterity or Strength to improve their Pact of the Blade fighting ability, but otherwise are interchangeable outside of lore and class mechanics.

Wizards, as expected, use Intelligence. Constitution might help holding spells. Wisdom might help with making decisions. Illusion and Enchanting Wizards, in particular, might use Charisma to help them manipulate people.

Pick a race. Picking one that's well built for a class (like Wood Elves and Monks) can be very cliche, but can give you an advantage in combat, if that's what you're looking for.

If you are worried about skills, pick your background next before choosing your class skills. Otherwise, you'll have to go back and redo some of the skills your background already gave you.

Pick your skills from your class

Pick your spells (if your class is a spellcaster). Having multiple options for ranged attacks (like Firebolt and Acid Splash) isn't a bad idea, but don't bother picking ALL of them since you really only need one alternative in case the enemy is resistant to something.
